rejected.argument:
Four findings against scripts/_b9_C09.py. I verified all four against primary sources before touching the file: I re-downloaded Hall's Secret Teachings (archive item the-secret-teachings-of-all-ages_202012, 314,505 words), pulled the Todorova PDF from revistas.ucm.es, and fetched the Google Arts & Culture asset page for the Psalter map. Three findings are real and are applied; one is flatly false and is rejected with evidence.

Applied, with corrections. (1) The Hall uniqueness claim was indeed false and I confirmed the counter-passages myself, but the finding misattributes the concentric geocentric chart to Fludd. Hall's text credits it to Georgius von Welling's Writings of 1735, reproduced via Hargrave Jennings, and Hall himself calls it "a Ptolemaic chart"; had I pasted the proposed fix I would have swapped one bad attribution for another in the same field the finding was written to protect. I applied the substance with the right author, quoted the actual ring labels and the music-of-the-spheres sentence against ourselves, and left the flat-Earth-relevant absence properly scoped to "the text searched". (2) Todorova's section 4 sentence is real, and omitting it while quoting the adjacent line was selective quotation of our own cited scholar; it is now in the steelman kernel in the affirmative. The finding's proposed answer asserts flatly that her "spheres of the created Universe" ARE the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic spheres, which her own footnotes do not support (she routes the reading through Maximus, Evdokimov, Plotinus and Pseudo-Dionysius's angelic hierarchy). I grounded the same conclusion in her section 2 instead, where she puts "Plato, Aristotle, Ptolemy and Plotinus on the structure of cosmos, sphericity of Earth" at the centre of Byzantine church writing — same destination, sourced. I also softened the preceding darkening paragraph, which as written argued the concentric mandorla is "the wrong way for a cosmos" and so contradicted the concession one paragraph later. (3) The Westminster Abbey attribution is wrong exactly as described; the page credits Fundación Elkano of Getaria and the manuscript is BL Add MS 28681. Because the advocate's preemptive marks that sentence load-bearing, I did not leave it resting on an exhibit caption: I found independent peer-reviewed corroboration (Grčić 2021, "With his left hand, Jesus holds a small T-O globe as a Pantocrator") and added it. On the date I did not do what was asked — see rejected/notes.

Rejected. The finding that the "not that none exists" concession clause is missing is simply false. It is in the file at the exact point claimed, and the reviewer's supporting claims are false too: they assert they "confirmed the substring is absent by evaluating the module" and that batch 9 is not yet wired into deep.py. Both are wrong, and I checked rather than assumed.

No edit made; applying the proposed fix would have produced a duplicated clause.

The finding is right that "All six" is a defect, and I narrowed it. But its stated basis and its proposed sentence both over-reach in the same direction: it says Planck's "uncontested" sentence is introduced by an enumeration that includes low variance. It is not. The enumeration in Planck 2018 VII sect. 6 is "a lack of large-angle correlations, a hemispherical power asymmetry ..., a preference for odd-parity modes ..., and an unexpectedly large temperature decrement in the southern hemisphere" - four items, of which three are E02's (339, 341, 326). Low variance (item 342) is not in that sentence's referent; it is treated in sect. 5 and reported at about the 1% level, and there is no 6.x subsection for it. So "Four of these six ... its isotropy paper calls their existence 'uncontested'" would attribute to that sentence one item it does not cover. I applied the correct count (four real features) but split the warrant: three named as 'uncontested', the fourth (low variance) as measured by Planck at about 1%.

rejected.argument: All five findings in unit E08 were checked against primary sources before editing (Anderson et al. 2002 full text via arXiv gr-qc/0104064; Turyshev et al. 2011 arXiv:1107.2886 and 2012 arXiv:1204.2507 full texts; Anderson & Nieto arXiv:0907.2469; Iorio arXiv:1311.4218 abstract and submission history; the archive.org OCR of Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II; the flyby encounter table with perigee altitudes). All five were substantially correct and were applied. One sub-claim inside finding 1's proposed replacement was rejected: it asserted that the CMB rest frame and the co-moving cosmological coordinate frame are "two different frames" and that the book's substitution is "a real, small misrendering". In FLRW cosmology the co-moving frame is operationally defined as the frame in which the CMB dipole vanishes, so the substitution is the standard identification, not an error; applying that half of the proposal would have replaced one false accusation with a weaker one. The straw_man block now withdraws the false absence claim entirely and records that Claim #5 is the book reporting Anderson et al. 2002 Sec. XI C (Rosales and Sanchez-Gomez) accurately, with the straw man confined to the Claim #1 response about the ephemeris. Finding 3's overstatement was tracked to five places, not the three the finding named (tldr, refutation section 1, refutation section 6, steelman KERNEL, advocate.best_defense, compression.note) and all were brought into line with what the papers actually say. Research notes 4, 6 and 8 in the module docstring were updated so the next agent does not reintroduce any of the five defects. File parses; no other file touched.
rejected.why: The proposal directed that the replacement sentence state that the book 'substitutes "Cosmic Microwave Background rest frame" for the paper's "co-moving cosmological coordinate frame" — two different frames' and that this is 'a real, small misrendering'. It is not. In FLRW cosmology the co-moving frame is the frame in which the CMB dipole vanishes; identifying the co-moving cosmological frame with the CMB rest frame is the standard operational move, and Rosales and Sanchez-Gomez's own argument is about the frame of the cosmic expansion, which is that frame. Writing the substitution up as a misrendering would have swapped a false accusation for an unsupportable one on a page whose subject is exactly that failure mode. The correction of the false absence claim — the substantive half of the finding — was applied in full, and the block now credits the book with reporting the position accurately.

rejected.argument:
Both findings that fall inside my file were verified against primary sources and applied — one of them with a corrected number, because the proposed replacement text carried a new arithmetic error. The third finding is valid but addresses scripts/clusters.py, which I do not own; it goes to the integrator.

FINDING 1 (referent) — CONFIRMED by fetching the cited URL. The University of Portsmouth / RAS release is headlined "Is Earth inside a huge void? 'Sound of the Big Bang' hints at possible solution to Hubble tension" and states in its own voice: "Earth and our solar system would need to be near the centre of a void about a billion light-years in radius and with a density about 20 per cent below the average." Our TLDR's punchline ("says 'our galaxy', not 'the Earth'") sent a reader to a page whose title appeared to refute it. Applied as the reviewer framed it: the drift is real but begins in the science communication, and the list inherited rather than invented it — which is a stronger finding for this project than the original.

FINDING 2 (15 Mpc scope) — CONFIRMED against the ar5iv full text of astro-ph/0607334, section V. Three sentences after the 15 Mpc bound: "When compared to the size of the underdensity, which according to Fig. 2 is around 1500 Mpc, this means that if we are placed at a random position inside the bubble, there is roughly a chance of 1 to 10^6..." The paper closes calling these LTB models "an exotic alternative to dark energy" (transition point d_0 = 1.34/1.68 Gpc, Table 1), so the bound is for a dark-energy-replacing bubble ~5x the ~300 Mpc void this cluster is about. The insensitivity argument was added so the conclusion no longer rests on the number, and the circular preemptive was rewritten to point at insensitivity rather than restating 49 million light-years.

PARTIAL REJECTION inside finding 2: its suggested sentence said the tolerance "would have to tighten by more than fifteen orders of magnitude". That is wrong. 15 Mpc / 1 AU = 3.09e12, i.e. 12.49 decades. The text says "more than twelve orders of magnitude" and the docstring records why.

Two further errors I found in my own file while editing there and fixed: 15 Mpc is a RADIUS, but three passages described the permitted volume as "a ball 49 million light-years wide" / "3.6e16 Earth diameters wide" / "a region 49 million light-years across" — a factor-of-two overstatement in our favour. Reworded to radius language.
rejected.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim / refutation §7 - the magnitude in finding 2's proposed text
rejected.why: The finding is right and I applied it, but its suggested sentence - "the tolerance would have to tighten by more than fifteen orders of magnitude" - is arithmetically wrong, and writing it would have replaced one defect with another. The finding itself supplies the two numbers that refute it: 15 Mpc against an Earth-Sun distance of 5e-12 Mpc is a ratio of 3.09e12, i.e. 12.49 orders of magnitude, not more than fifteen. The text as written says "more than twelve orders of magnitude" and docstring note 6 records the correction so a later pass does not reintroduce it.

rejected.argument:
I owned scripts/_b9_E12.py only. I verified all three findings against primary text rather than accepting them: I pulled the exact Internet Archive OCR the entry names (Galileo Was Wrong, vol 1-3 complete, 5,499,250 bytes / 134,983 lines — byte-and-line identical to the docstring's claim) and the creation.com PDF of Humphreys TJ 16(2). Two findings held and were applied with corrections; the third was substantially wrong and I rejected its central claim while fixing the one real error buried in it.

Finding 1 (major, "all three speeds") is correct: the galactocentric frame is two subtractions, and Bajan et al. give "galactocentric ... or ... CMB", so the body outran the TLDR. Applied. The finding's second half — that the source's own printed rebuttal at Vol. II ch. 10, p. 298 goes unmet — also checked out; I located the passage in the OCR at line 62678, printed p. 298, chapter header "Chapter 10: Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentrism", inside Volume II (which begins at line 45232, "Chapters 7 to 13"). I answered it from the book's own pages rather than from the finding's proposed footnote citation, which is misquoted: the p. 417 footnote prints "Global Redshift Periodicities: Association with the Cosmic Background Radiation," Astrophysics and Space Science 239, 35 (1996) and "Evidence for Quantized and Variable Redshifts in the CBR Rest Frame," Astrophysics and Space Science, 1997 — it does not print "J. Astrophys. Astr. 18:415, 1997". I trimmed the Bennett quote to 56 words (the finding's version is 72, over the 60-word cap) and I did not attribute the chapter to Bennett alone, since Vol. II's title page names both authors.

Finding 2 (cluster note renders as the basis line) is correct on every checkable point: build.py:156 sets "basis": c["note"], clusters.py:598 carries the note that section IV explicitly refuses, and the docstring's "(see note 4)" did point at the wrong note. clusters.py untouched; the report-up list now names the note, carries the proposed basis and real_source verbatim, and warns the integrator to anchor on the "E12" key.

Finding 3 (major, "the Sungenis-to-Humphreys link is asserted rather than shown") is wrong, and its proposed fix would have deleted a true and load-bearing claim. Its two supporting assertions both fail against the OCR it cites. (a) "None of Humphreys' geometry, arithmetic or one-in-a-trillion figure is located anywhere in that text": printed p. 432 block-quotes Humphreys' equation (15) passage almost verbatim — the ratio of volumes, "where R is the minimum radius of the cosmos estimated by observation, say about 20 billion light years. Using 6r = 1.6 million light years ... the probability of our galaxy being so close to the centre of the cosmos by accident is less than one out of a trillion" — introduced as "As one cosmologist put it:" with the footnote at the foot of that page citing Humphreys' paper by title. I confirmed word-for-word correspondence against Humphreys' own PDF (his eq. 15 passage). (b) "No figure caption crediting Humphreys is located in it either": p. 431 reproduces his Figure 8, panels "(a) Viewed from centre (b) 2 million light-years from centre" with the axis "Distance (Millions of Light-Years)" — Humphreys' PDF Figure 8 is "Computer-simulated effect of our viewpoint on galaxy distance groups. (a) ... (b) The same groups seen from a place 2 million light-years away from the centre" — and p. 296 carries an explicit credit line, "Above picture courtesy of R. Humphrey's article 'Our Galaxy is at the Centre of the Universe, "Quantized" Redshifts Show' in Journal of Creation 16(2):95-104". So the chain claim is documented, not asserted, and I strengthened the gloss with the page numbers instead of withdrawing it. The finding is right on one narrow point — "cites twice by title" is an undercount — but its own count is also wrong: the title occurs seven times (pp. 284, 296, 398, 432, 580, 631, 694), not six; the finding missed the p. 296 credit, which is the very instance that disproves its figure claim. The finding is also right that the section quoted in `passage` (pp. 417-420) argues from Tifft, Sky & Telescope, Matthews and Koo/Kron and contains no Humphreys — but the derivation is fourteen pages later in the same chapter, so "argues in parallel with it" is false.

One repair outside the findings: compression.note's "a scope is widened by about nine orders of magnitude" is a quantifier nothing in the body supports (galaxy diameter to planet diameter is ~14 orders, not 9, and no other reading of the comparison lands on 9). Since the finding put that sentence in play anyway, I replaced the number with the non-numeric claim the paragraph actually proves.

rejected.argument:
Two of three findings were mine to fix and both were real; I applied both, but finding 1's factual premise about Park et al. 2017 was itself wrong and I fixed the entry to what the paper actually says rather than to what the finding proposed. Finding 3 is a clusters.py defect I am forbidden to touch, so it goes to the integrator with a concrete, anchor-safe handoff written into my own docstring.

I downloaded and read the Park et al. 2017 PDF (AJ 153:121, MIT DSpace bitstream) rather than reasoning from memory, and it settles the disputed points. (a) The finding's claim that Park et al. "decouple the effects of beta and J2 by taking gamma from the Cassini Shapiro-delay result rather than fitting the PPN parameters and J2 together" is half right and half wrong: gamma is indeed not estimated ("Instead, we constrain the value of γ to the Cassini experiment value"; the solar angular momentum Se is likewise held to the helioseismic value), but beta and J2 ARE estimated together in one least-squares fit from the MESSENGER ranging data. (b) The actual degeneracy-breaker is stronger than either the finding or the old text: the fit does not rest on the secular residual at all. Equation 4 of the paper gives the periodic change in Mercury's argument of perihelion within a single orbit as a function of beta and gamma only, with maximum amplitude ~22.6 km against metre-level ranging, while "the periodic amplitude due to solar oblateness is several orders of magnitude smaller than the GE effect and is out of phase". So beta is read off an observable J2 barely touches. That is a direct answer to Dicke, who was arguing about the secular residual. (c) There is a genuinely Mercury-free second measurement with a number: Pijpers 1998 (MNRAS 297:L76) gets J2 = (2.18 ± 0.06) × 10⁻⁷ from the helioseismic rotation profile, and Park et al. themselves note their 2.25 × 10⁻⁷ "is in good agreement with the expected value from the helioseismology value". The old steelman's "twice, by methods that do not use Mercury" was false as written; the corrected version concedes the joint fit and then wins on the merits, which is a better page than the one that dodged.

On finding 2, I checked the arithmetic before asserting it: summing the four giant planets' maximum contributions gives 1,509,476 km = 2.17 solar radii for the largest possible solar-system barycentre excursion, and 1 AU is 99 times that. Those are the numbers now in the text.
rejected.field: finding 1 - the characterisation of Park et al. 2017
rejected.why: The finding states the paper's authors "decouple the effects of beta and J2 by taking gamma from the Cassini Shapiro-delay result rather than fitting the PPN parameters and J2 together", and instructs me to write that Park et al. "solved for beta and J2 separately". That is wrong about the paper and would have introduced a new error in place of the old one. Park et al. Table 1 reports "the recovered values of J2 and β from processing MESSENGER ranging data using a least-squares estimation technique" - beta and J2 come out of the same fit, jointly. What is imported from outside is gamma ("Instead, we constrain the value of γ to the Cassini experiment value") and the solar angular momentum Se (a priori from helioseismology). Writing "they solved for beta and J2 separately" would have handed a reader who opens the PDF an immediate refutation of our refutation, on the exact page where the entry claims its strongest answer. I applied the finding's intent - answer the circularity charge honestly - using the paper's real mechanism, which is stronger: the periodic argument-of-perihelion signal (Eq. 4) depends on beta and gamma alone, so the joint fit is not the circular one Dicke's objection describes.

record_problems.argument:
Both C06 findings were sound and both were applied, after verifying the underlying source directly. I pulled Gutenberg #69892 and read Section 8 in full: the finding's characterisation of the first half is accurate (lines 1830-1841 argue light through "a dense medium ... will appear larger" and that the low Sun "must be dilated or enlarged as well as modified in colour"), and the entry really was quoting around it, taking only the Phillips footnote from the section's second half. So the standard atmospheric-magnification escape was left open against the entry's single best measurement, exactly as the reviewer said.

One thing the finding did not notice, and it strengthens rather than weakens the fix: Rowbotham's very next sentence after the "dilated or enlarged" passage declines the escape himself - "the enlarged appearance of the Sun when rising and setting is only an optical impression, as proved by actual measurement" - which is the sentence the Phillips footnote exists to support. Under the hedge rule that sentence has to be quoted through rather than stopped at, in both directions, so the new paragraph quotes the dense-medium reasoning, notes that Rowbotham does not take that road, and then answers the modern defender's version on optics anyway (refraction lifts rather than magnifies, lifts the lower limb more than the upper, flattens the disc vertically by roughly 5 arcmin while leaving the horizontal diameter alone; compensation needed is a factor of about twelve at 5 degrees, not a few per cent, and would have to track altitude on every clear day at every latitude). Numbers were checked: 1/sin(5 deg) = 11.5, and the ~1/6 flattening is confirmed by a citable source I fetched and verified (Andrew T. Young, SDSU), which I added to the sources list.

On the TLDR: "in the books it comes from" is a descent claim, and the entry refuses to make one everywhere else (module docstring "is in print thirty years before the Zion sermons"; refutation "It is NOT offered as the route"; compression note "the entry does not claim it"). The reviewer's replacement - a located-earliest claim - is exactly what the entry proves, so I took it with em-dash punctuation to match house style.

I kept survives=4 rather than raising it: the new advocate move is answered in the body as shipped, which is the stated criterion in preemptive. I renumbered the closing advocate move to "Fifth and last", retired the brittle "first and fourth moves" phrasing in preemptive for named moves, and added the (e) note so a future pass cannot trim the optics paragraph without noticing what it defends.

Nothing rejected. Python syntax verified with ast.parse and the module imports cleanly; no test/build/git run.

record_problems.argument:
Four findings against scripts/_b9_C09.py. I verified all four against primary sources before touching the file: I re-downloaded Hall's Secret Teachings (archive item the-secret-teachings-of-all-ages_202012, 314,505 words), pulled the Todorova PDF from revistas.ucm.es, and fetched the Google Arts & Culture asset page for the Psalter map. Three findings are real and are applied; one is flatly false and is rejected with evidence.

Applied, with corrections. (1) The Hall uniqueness claim was indeed false and I confirmed the counter-passages myself, but the finding misattributes the concentric geocentric chart to Fludd. Hall's text credits it to Georgius von Welling's Writings of 1735, reproduced via Hargrave Jennings, and Hall himself calls it "a Ptolemaic chart"; had I pasted the proposed fix I would have swapped one bad attribution for another in the same field the finding was written to protect. I applied the substance with the right author, quoted the actual ring labels and the music-of-the-spheres sentence against ourselves, and left the flat-Earth-relevant absence properly scoped to "the text searched". record_problems.argument:
All four D19 findings were checked against primary sources before anything was edited, and all four survived. Three were applied in scripts/_b9_D19.py; the fourth targets clusters.py, which I do not own, so it is escalated verbatim.

Finding 1 (Metonic/Saros misidentification) is correct and was the load-bearing error on the page. Fetching sacred-texts za29.htm confirms the 1881 recipe's own next clause: repetitions "have occurred in every cycle of between eighteen and nineteen years", illustrated by an express train passing "of every eighteenth day". The "nineteenth and twentieth years" are rows of an annual table, so the bracketed interval is ~18 years, and the same chapter has already named that interval in the Partington quotation as the Saros of 6,585 1/3 days. I also re-ran the keyword search myself rather than trusting the finding: downloading PG #69892 gives metonic 0, meton 0, draconic 0, nineteen 0, against saros 1, node 1, apogee 1. So the chapter supplies two of the four quantities the list names (node, Saros) plus one it does not (apogee), and I narrowed every downstream overclaim to that count.

On the finding's two-way fix for item 365 I took the conservative branch. I verified the FES wiki does carry a Metonic reference — "Keith says 'The cycle of the moon is said to have been discovered by Meton, an Athenian in B.C. 433,'" attributed to T. G. Ferguson, Earth Review, September 1894 — but that is a remark about who discovered the cycle, not about its precision, so routing item 365 there would be substituting a different guess. I recorded it as the nearest Metonic reference located in any carrier cited on the page and marked item 365 untraced.

Finding 2 is correct and the sentence it attacks was genuinely refutable in one click. Carpenter's proof 66 (PG #55387) reads: "It is often said that the predictions of eclipses prove astronomers to be right in their theories. But it is not seen that this proves too much. It is well known that Ptolemy predicted eclipses for six-hundred years, on the basis of a plane Earth..." The technical vocabulary did not travel through Carpenter; the argument did. I additionally verified the shared Ptolemy/600-years detail in Rowbotham's own chapter, footnoted to Smith's Rise and Progress of Astronomy, which strengthens the finding beyond what it claimed. The "distributors return to the same few originals" inference no longer followed from this case and was dropped.

Finding 4 is correct: survives=4 obliges an answer in the body, and the answer sat only in preemptive, which build.py strips. I confirmed the trap the finding names — EclipseWise states ELP-2000/82 "contains a total of 37862 periodic terms" — so I quote that number ourselves and spend it, rather than leaving a defender to find it in a source we cite. Section seven now argues the fitted/derived ratio explicitly and cross-references Clairaut; section eight now scopes Delta-T as one scalar function of time.

Nothing was rejected. The only deviations from the proposed fixes are the untraced branch on item 365 and the refusal to edit clusters.py.

record_problems.argument:
All three findings for E04 survive verification against primary sources, and I applied all three — but with the proposed fixes tightened where they themselves overstated. FINDING 1 (mutual-exclusivity claim) — CONFIRMED and applied. I verified from the Internet Archive OCR of Galileo Was Wrong (/tmp/gww_flat.txt) that Sungenis's model is explicitly a universe rotating diurnally about a fixed Earth ("if space is rotating diurnally every 24 hours around the Earth"; "the daily rotation of the universe"; "a rotating universe around a fixed Earth"), with an annual precession besides. A rotating cosmos has a centre and an axis. So "a central Earth in a spherically symmetric cosmos... predicts no preferred direction at all" was false about the source, and "at most one of these items can be evidence for a central Earth" was a technicality the source never walked into. Withdrawn in six places (gloss 1, refutation opening, refutation VIII, steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, verdict_challenge.reasoning, docstring note 1) and replaced with the weaker true claim: two unrelated results spliced by "in other words". The advocate's actual hit ("It is a rotation about an axis. An axis is what we claimed") is now answered in advocate.preemptive (a) by redirecting to IV(a),(c),(d) rather than to the logical point. FINDING 2 (the "changes subject to quasars" accusation) — CONFIRMED and applied. I located the introducing sentence in the scan verbatim: "Lastly, a team studying the orientation of quasars has discovered that they have a preferred axis, the same as they found for radio wavelengths and micro wavelengths (i.e., the CMB)." The book names the CMB in its own voice on printed p. 413, one sentence before the block quote. And Urban & Zhitnitsky's p. 2 does argue a single common axis: II.A "tend to identify an axis in the sky which closely align with the direction of the cosmological dipole"; II.B "single out a preferred axis, again coinciding with the cosmological dipole"; II.C the quadrupole/octopole normals. So the entry's self-declared hardest finding was overreach. The mechanical part (ellipsis removes the subject; "[sun-earth]" glosses the ecliptic) is kept; the accusation is withdrawn and section V now answers the claim on its merits with the footnote-9 coordinates (A1–A3 at lII 267, bII 69; CMB dipole at lII 264, bII 48), the "definitely affected by observational biases" passage, and Urban & Zhitnitsky's own footnote 2 ("mere coincidence"). Item 117's strongest form is now in steelman.description and in advocate.best_defense. The ecliptic-frame gap is stated scoped: "ecliptic" returns zero hits in the text of astro-ph/0507274 as searched (verified: 0 occurrences, vs 4 for "supergalactic"), so IV(d) rebuts an equatorial-frame axis and no ecliptic-frame test is reported either way in the papers cited here. FINDING 3 (IV(b) handedness) — CONFIRMED and applied, with one correction to the finding's own framing. The abstract of astro-ph/0507274 does say "These characteristics make the alignment effect difficult to explain in terms of local mechanisms, namely a contamination by interstellar polarization in our Galaxy" — the exact reverse of the deleted sentence. The body hedges verified verbatim: "a counter-clockwise rotation in both the South and North Galactic Caps (S2 symmetry) cannot be totally excluded"; "both the slope and the constant of the linear fit depend on the coordinate system"; "due to the 180 degree uncertainty, several other complicated or asymmetric solutions... could be imagined"; the z=0 step-like discontinuity "is due to the way position angles are defined on the celestial sphere"; and "The mirror-like symmetry of the θ̄ − z relation... would be accounted for by a rotation axis close to the A1–A3 axis". IV(b) is now a stated withdrawal that carries the paper's hedges and its rotating-cosmology reading; the TLDR's handedness clause is gone; advocate.preemptive (b) now pins the correction instead of the error. Section IV's intro was adjusted so "four features" no longer promises four usable ones, and the same handedness argument was removed from steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, which finding 3 did not list but which carried the identical defect. Python parses; all

/

Verification performed (arXiv full text + the Internet Archive scan, fetched and searched this session):
1. Titles. arXiv:0707.3793 and arXiv:0904.2529 both carry the title "Evidence for a Preferred Handedness of Spiral Galaxies" (confirmed by search result titles for both abs pages; a separate earlier Longo paper, astro-ph/0703325, is the one titled "Does the Universe Have a Handedness?"). The published paper is "Detection of a Dipole in the Handedness of Spiral Galaxies with Redshifts z ~ 0.04", PLB 699 (2011). So the gloss's old sentence about the book "printing the 2007 title" described nothing that exists — finding 3's premise is right.
2. The 5 sigma figure. arXiv:1104.2815 (the published version) full text contains verbatim: "Overall the asymmetry is -0.0607 +/- 0.0118, a 5.15 sigma effect with a probability of 2.5x10-7 for occurring by chance", and "The 165 deg < alpha < 225 deg sector with 86% of the galaxies shows an asymmetry of -0.0695 +/- 0.0127, a 5.48 sigma effect", with sectors "195 deg +/- 30 deg and 15 deg +/- 30 deg". The same paper's unbinned fit states "No a priori assumptions about the direction of the dipole axis or its magnitude were made", giving 7.9 x 10^-4. So the book's quoted "signal exceeding 5 sigma" survives into the refereed article intact and was not a dropped qualifier — finding 2 is right, and "the significance halves" was also arithmetically false (5.15 -> 3.16).
3. The book's footnotes. Downloaded the seventh-edition djvu text from the Internet Archive item and located every hit for 0707.3793, 0904.2529 and 10.1016. Page positions were fixed by the footer digit that closes each page block in the OCR (verified against the structure "...text... / 383 / Chapter 3: ..."), not the running head. Confirmed: the footnote closing p. 384 quotes the 2009 preprint's abstract ("The new study uses 15,158 with redshifts <0.085 ... a signal exceeding 5 sigma") under the URL .../papers/0707/0707.3793.pdf, p. 9, then says "In a slightly different version of the same article" and gives 0904.2529; the footnote printed twice, closing pp. 240 and 448, reads "'Evidence for a Preferred Handedness of Spiral Galaxies,' Michael Longo, Physics Letters B 10.1016, 2009; http://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/0904/0904.2529.pdf". Finding 3's page numbers and text are exactly right. (An extra footnote closing p. 383 gives the title, "University of Michigan, 2009" and the 0707 URL — added to the docstring.)

Where I deviated. Finding 1's proposed replacement said "every re-analysis of Longo's and Shamir's own catalogues by other groups - Galaxy Zoo 2008, Hayes 2017, Iye 2021, Patel & Desmond 2024". That misdescribes two of the four: Galaxy Zoo 2008 classified its own ~37,000 SDSS spirals rather than re-analysing anyone's catalogue, and Hayes 2017 re-analysed Galaxy Zoo 1, not Longo or Shamir. Applying it verbatim would have swapped one defect for another. I used a named, closed set instead — "the four independent checks this page relies on - Galaxy Zoo 2008, Hayes 2017, Iye 2021 and Patel & Desmond 2024 ... each came back consistent with isotropy" - plus the concession sentence the finding rightly demanded.

One adjacent fix not in the findings but the same defect class: the verdict paragraph closed "the two decades of re-analysis since have gone one way", an unqualified universal of exactly the kind the TLDR finding targets, sitting one paragraph after section seven concedes the exchange is open. Narrowed to "every re-analysis listed above has gone one way - with the exchange described in section seven still open."

record_problems.argument: All five findings in unit E08 were checked against primary sources before editing (Anderson et al. 2002 full text via arXiv gr-qc/0104064; Turyshev et al. 2011 arXiv:1107.2886 and 2012 arXiv:1204.2507 full texts; Anderson & Nieto arXiv:0907.2469; Iorio arXiv:1311.4218 abstract and submission history; the archive.org OCR of Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II; the flyby encounter table with perigee altitudes). All five were substantially correct and were applied. One sub-claim inside finding 1's proposed replacement was rejected: it asserted that the CMB rest frame and the co-moving cosmological coordinate frame are "two different frames" and that the book's substitution is "a real, small misrendering". In FLRW cosmology the co-moving frame is operationally defined as the frame in which the CMB dipole vanishes, so the substitution is the standard identification, not an error; applying that half of the proposal would have replaced one false accusation with a weaker one. The straw_man block now withdraws the false absence claim entirely and records that Claim #5 is the book reporting Anderson et al. 2002 Sec. XI C (Rosales and Sanchez-Gomez) accurately, with the straw man confined to the Claim #1 response about the ephemeris. Finding 3's overstatement was tracked to five places, not the three the finding named (tldr, refutation section 1, refutation section 6, steelman KERNEL, advocate.best_defense, compression.note) and all were brought into line with what the papers actually say. Research notes 4, 6 and 8 in the module docstring were updated so the next agent does not reintroduce any of the five defects. File parses; no other file touched.

FINDING 1 (referent) — CONFIRMED by fetching the cited URL. The University of Portsmouth / RAS release is headlined "Is Earth inside a huge void? 'Sound of the Big Bang' hints at possible solution to Hubble tension" and states in its own voice: "Earth and our solar system would need to be near the centre of a void about a billion light-years in radius and with a density about 20 per cent below the average." Our TLDR's punchline ("says 'our galaxy', not 'the Earth'") sent a reader to a page whose title appeared to refute it. Applied as the reviewer framed it: the drift is real but begins in the science communication, and the list inherited rather than invented it — which is a stronger finding for this project than the original.

FINDING 2 (15 Mpc scope) — CONFIRMED against the ar5iv full text of astro-ph/0607334, section V. Three sentences after the 15 Mpc bound: "When compared to the size of the underdensity, which according to Fig. 2 is around 1500 Mpc, this means that if we are placed at a random position inside the bubble, there is roughly a chance of 1 to 10^6..." The paper closes calling these LTB models "an exotic alternative to dark energy" (transition point d_0 = 1.34/1.68 Gpc, Table 1), so the bound is for a dark-energy-replacing bubble ~5x the ~300 Mpc void this cluster is about. The insensitivity argument was added so the conclusion no longer rests on the number, and the circular preemptive was rewritten to point at insensitivity rather than restating 49 million light-years.

PARTIAL REJECTION inside finding 2: its suggested sentence said the tolerance "would have to tighten by more than fifteen orders of magnitude". That is wrong. 15 Mpc / 1 AU = 3.09e12, i.e. 12.49 decades. The text says "more than twelve orders of magnitude" and the docstring records why.

Two further errors I found in my own file while editing there and fixed: 15 Mpc is a RADIUS, but three passages described the permitted volume as "a ball 49 million light-years wide" / "3.6e16 Earth diameters wide" / "a region 49 million light-years across" — a factor-of-two overstatement in our favour. Reworded to radius language.
record_problems.problem: FINDING 3, VALID, NOT MINE TO FIX - scripts/clusters.py, cluster E09 `note`. Current text: "The local-void reading was tested directly on 1295 supernovae and excluded at 4-5σ." This is a published overstatement, not merely stale. Kenworthy, Scolnic & Riess 2019 (ApJ 875:145) exclude at 4-5σ specifically sharp-edged LTB underdensities with |delta| > 20% (5σ bound delta < 27% on scales above 69 h^-1 Mpc, 1295 SNe over 0.01 < z < 2.26). They do not close the local-void reading, which is argued in MNRAS by Banik & Kalaitzidis (540:545, 2025) and which §5, §6 and the TLDR of this entry deliberately leave open. The note renders as the basis line beside the verdict chip (scripts/render.py line 180), so skim readers who never expand the entry meet the one claim the body refuses to make. Suggested replacement, which the body does support: "Two rival explanations of one number, counted as two proofs. Kenworthy et al. 2019 exclude sharp-edged voids deeper than 20% at 4-5σ on 1295 supernovae; a shallower local void is still argued in MNRAS. Either way the region is tens to hundreds of megaparsecs across and does not single out the Earth." Anchor the edit on the cluster key "E09", never on a line number. This also needs an entry in review/corrections.json - it is a correction of a published claim, not a wording tidy. I did not touch clusters.py, render.py or corrections.json.

record_problems.argument:
Two of three findings were mine to fix and both were real; I applied both, but finding 1's factual premise about Park et al. 2017 was itself wrong and I fixed the entry to what the paper actually says rather than to what the finding proposed. Finding 3 is a clusters.py defect I am forbidden to touch, so it goes to the integrator with a concrete, anchor-safe handoff written into my own docstring.

I downloaded and read the Park et al. 2017 PDF (AJ 153:121, MIT DSpace bitstream) rather than reasoning from memory, and it settles the disputed points. (a) The finding's claim that Park et al. "decouple the effects of beta and J2 by taking gamma from the Cassini Shapiro-delay result rather than fitting the PPN parameters and J2 together" is half right and half wrong: gamma is indeed not estimated ("Instead, we constrain the value of γ to the Cassini experiment value"; the solar angular momentum Se is likewise held to the helioseismic value), but beta and J2 ARE estimated together in one least-squares fit from the MESSENGER ranging data. (b) The actual degeneracy-breaker is stronger than either the finding or the old text: the fit does not rest on the secular residual at all. Equation 4 of the paper gives the periodic change in Mercury's argument of perihelion within a single orbit as a function of beta and gamma only, with maximum amplitude ~22.6 km against metre-level ranging, while "the periodic amplitude due to solar oblateness is several orders of magnitude smaller than the GE effect and is out of phase". So beta is read off an observable J2 barely touches. That is a direct answer to Dicke, who was arguing about the secular residual. (c) There is a genuinely Mercury-free second measurement with a number: Pijpers 1998 (MNRAS 297:L76) gets J2 = (2.18 ± 0.06) × 10⁻⁷ from the helioseismic rotation profile, and Park et al. themselves note their 2.25 × 10⁻⁷ "is in good agreement with the expected value from the helioseismology value". The old steelman's "twice, by methods that do not use Mercury" was false as written; the corrected version concedes the joint fit and then wins on the merits, which is a better page than the one that dodged.

On finding 2, I checked the arithmetic before asserting it: summing the four giant planets' maximum contributions gives 1,509,476 km = 2.17 solar radii for the largest possible solar-system barycentre excursion, and 1 AU is 99 times that. Those are the numbers now in the text.
record_problems.problem: scripts/clusters.py, key "E14": originator=None, originator_work=None, year=None, real_source=None, while the treatment beneath opens with a Sungenis & Bennett passage (WRK-SUNGENIS-2006), people=["PER-SUNGENIS"], and four page-located matches in one volume. render.py prints "· no named originator" into the meta line directly above the entry, so the summary contradicts the treatment before a reader expands it. Requested: leave originator/originator_work/year as None - a content match is not a transmission chain and naming an originator on this evidence violates the three-state rule - but set real_source to the located parallel with its caveat, e.g. "Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I (2006) - parallel located, descent not demonstrated", and carry the caveat in the note: four of the five items have a page-located counterpart in that volume (oblateness at printed pp. 1003-1004, apex at p. 959, barycentre at pp. 198-199 and 598-603); item 192 (neutrinos) has no counterpart in the Vol. I full text searched and stays untraced; the list carries no citations, so descent is not demonstrated.

Finding 3's diagnosis is therefore right and slightly understated — the page was excluding a class in section four and illustrating the prize with a specimen that survives that particular leg of the test. per_unit.argument:
Both C06 findings were sound and both were applied, after verifying the underlying source directly. I pulled Gutenberg #69892 and read Section 8 in full: the finding's characterisation of the first half is accurate (lines 1830-1841 argue light through "a dense medium ... will appear larger" and that the low Sun "must be dilated or enlarged as well as modified in colour"), and the entry really was quoting around it, taking only the Phillips footnote from the section's second half. So the standard atmospheric-magnification escape was left open against the entry's single best measurement, exactly as the reviewer said.

One thing the finding did not notice, and it strengthens rather than weakens the fix: Rowbotham's very next sentence after the "dilated or enlarged" passage declines the escape himself - "the enlarged appearance of the Sun when rising and setting is only an optical impression, as proved by actual measurement" - which is the sentence the Phillips footnote exists to support. Under the hedge rule that sentence has to be quoted through rather than stopped at, in both directions, so the new paragraph quotes the dense-medium reasoning, notes that Rowbotham does not take that road, and then answers the modern defender's version on optics anyway (refraction lifts rather than magnifies, lifts the lower limb more than the upper, flattens the disc vertically by roughly 5 arcmin while leaving the horizontal diameter alone; compensation needed is a factor of about twelve at 5 degrees, not a few per cent, and would have to track altitude on every clear day at every latitude). Numbers were checked: 1/sin(5 deg) = 11.5, and the ~1/6 flattening is confirmed by a citable source I fetched and verified (Andrew T. Young, SDSU), which I added to the sources list.

On the TLDR: "in the books it comes from" is a descent claim, and the entry refuses to make one everywhere else (module docstring "is in print thirty years before the Zion sermons"; refutation "It is NOT offered as the route"; compression note "the entry does not claim it"). The reviewer's replacement - a located-earliest claim - is exactly what the entry proves, so I took it with em-dash punctuation to match house style.

I kept survives=4 rather than raising it: the new advocate move is answered in the body as shipped, which is the stated criterion in preemptive. I renumbered the closing advocate move to "Fifth and last", retired the brittle "first and fourth moves" phrasing in preemptive for named moves, and added the (e) note so a future pass cannot trim the optics paragraph without noticing what it defends.

Nothing rejected. Python syntax verified with ast.parse and the module imports cleanly; no test/build/git run.

per_unit.argument:
Four findings against scripts/_b9_C09.py. I verified all four against primary sources before touching the file: I re-downloaded Hall's Secret Teachings (archive item the-secret-teachings-of-all-ages_202012, 314,505 words), pulled the Todorova PDF from revistas.ucm.es, and fetched the Google Arts & Culture asset page for the Psalter map. Three findings are real and are applied; one is flatly false and is rejected with evidence.

Applied, with corrections. (1) The Hall uniqueness claim was indeed false and I confirmed the counter-passages myself, but the finding misattributes the concentric geocentric chart to Fludd. Hall's text credits it to Georgius von Welling's Writings of 1735, reproduced via Hargrave Jennings, and Hall himself calls it "a Ptolemaic chart"; had I pasted the proposed fix I would have swapped one bad attribution for another in the same field the finding was written to protect. I applied the substance with the right author, quoted the actual ring labels and the music-of-the-spheres sentence against ourselves, and left the flat-Earth-relevant absence properly scoped to "the text searched". (2) Todorova's section 4 sentence is real, and omitting it while quoting the adjacent line was selective quotation of our own cited scholar; it is now in the steelman kernel in the affirmative. The finding's proposed answer asserts flatly that her "spheres of the created Universe" ARE the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic spheres, which her own footnotes do not support (she routes the reading through Maximus, Evdokimov, Plotinus and Pseudo-Dionysius's angelic hierarchy). I grounded the same conclusion in her section 2 instead, where she puts "Plato, Aristotle, Ptolemy and Plotinus on the structure of cosmos, sphericity of Earth" at the centre of Byzantine church writing — same destination, sourced. I also softened the preceding darkening paragraph, which as written argued the concentric mandorla is "the wrong way for a cosmos" and so contradicted the concession one paragraph later. (3) The Westminster Abbey attribution is wrong exactly as described; the page credits Fundación Elkano of Getaria and the manuscript is BL Add MS 28681. Because the advocate's preemptive marks that sentence load-bearing, I did not leave it resting on an exhibit caption: I found independent peer-reviewed corroboration (Grčić 2021, "With his left hand, Jesus holds a small T-O globe as a Pantocrator") and added it. On the date I did not do what was asked — see rejected/notes.

Rejected. The finding that the "not that none exists" concession clause is missing is simply false. It is in the file at the exact point claimed, and the reviewer's supporting claims are false too: they assert they "confirmed the substring is absent by evaluating the module" and that batch 9 is not yet wired into deep.py. per_unit.argument: All three findings in unit D14 were checked against primary sources before touching the file, and all three held up; none were rejected. (1) The MOND-scale arithmetic: with a0 = 1.2e-10 m/s^2 and GM_sun = 1.327e20, the Earth's orbital acceleration is 5.93e-3 m/s^2, a ratio of 4.9e7 (10^7.7), and Neptune's is 6.6e-6 m/s^2, a ratio of 5.5e4 (10^4.7). "Eleven orders" is the surface-gravity ratio (9.81/1.2e-10 = 8.2e10), which is not what either sentence was about, so both instances were wrong. I used the orbital figures in the steelman and the physical statement in the refutation, r = sqrt(GM_sun/a0) = 1.05e15 m = 7,030 AU, rounded to "roughly 7,000 AU". (2) I pulled the arXiv abstract of astro-ph/0606216 (Angus, Famaey & Zhao 2006): it is analytic potential-density pairs, orbits and lensing for semi-Hernquist baryonic profiles in three versions of MOND, generating "a weak lensing signal resembling that of the merging galaxy cluster 1E 0657-56". No neutrinos, no hot dark component. The neutrino move is astro-ph/0609125 (Angus, Shan, Zhao & Famaey), whose abstract proposes "the 'marriage' of MOND with ordinary hot neutrinos of 2eV" and whose journal ref I confirmed as ApJ 654:L13-L16 (2007), and 0805.4014 (Angus), confirmed via Crossref DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2966.2008.14341.x as MNRAS 394:527-532 (2009), titled at publication "Is an 11 eV sterile neutrino consistent with clusters, the cosmic microwave background and modified Newtonian dynamics?" — note the published title differs from the arXiv title the finding used, and I used the published one. So I kept Angus/Famaey/Zhao for the lensing modelling and moved the neutrino claim to its own two citations, in the refutation, the advocate block and the sources list. (3) Boran et al. falsify "dark matter emulators", defined in their own abstract as theories "which dispense with the need for dark matter by making ordinary matter couple to a different metric from that of GW" — so GW170817 killed the family where the two do NOT share a metric, and the old sentence stated the exact inverse, contradicting our own Skordis/Zlosnik source label ("gravitational waves at c"). Rewritten, with the mechanism named (their estimated ~400-day differential Shapiro delay against the observed 1.7 s) so the sentence carries its own check. I went slightly beyond the three findings in two bounded ways, both inside the same defect: I sharpened the Boran source label, which repeated the inverted claim as "what killed the earlier relativistic MOND", and I added a line to advocate.preemptive (d)/(c) warning an editor not to re-file the neutrino answer under Angus/Famaey/Zhao, since that is how the error got in. Syntax parses. No positional edits; every anchor was a unique string.

A rotating cosmos has a centre and an axis. So "a central Earth in a spherically symmetric cosmos... predicts no preferred direction at all" was false about the source, and "at most one of these items can be evidence for a central Earth" was a technicality the source never walked into. I located the introducing sentence in the scan verbatim: "Lastly, a team studying the orientation of quasars has discovered that they have a preferred axis, the same as they found for radio wavelengths and micro wavelengths (i.e., the CMB)." The book names the CMB in its own voice on printed p. 413, one sentence before the block quote. per_unit.argument:
All three findings for E05 survived verification against primary sources, so all three were applied — but finding 1's proposed replacement wording was itself wrong and I substituted a corrected version.

Verification performed (arXiv full text + the Internet Archive scan, fetched and searched this session):
1. Titles. arXiv:0707.3793 and arXiv:0904.2529 both carry the title "Evidence for a Preferred Handedness of Spiral Galaxies" (confirmed by search result titles for both abs pages; a separate earlier Longo paper, astro-ph/0703325, is the one titled "Does the Universe Have a Handedness?"). The published paper is "Detection of a Dipole in the Handedness of Spiral Galaxies with Redshifts z ~ 0.04", PLB 699 (2011). So the gloss's old sentence about the book "printing the 2007 title" described nothing that exists — finding 3's premise is right.
2. The 5 sigma figure. arXiv:1104.2815 (the published version) full text contains verbatim: "Overall the asymmetry is -0.0607 +/- 0.0118, a 5.15 sigma effect with a probability of 2.5x10-7 for occurring by chance", and "The 165 deg < alpha < 225 deg sector with 86% of the galaxies shows an asymmetry of -0.0695 +/- 0.0127, a 5.48 sigma effect", with sectors "195 deg +/- 30 deg and 15 deg +/- 30 deg". The same paper's unbinned fit states "No a priori assumptions about the direction of the dipole axis or its magnitude were made", giving 7.9 x 10^-4. So the book's quoted "signal exceeding 5 sigma" survives into the refereed article intact and was not a dropped qualifier — finding 2 is right, and "the significance halves" was also arithmetically false (5.15 -> 3.16).
3. The book's footnotes. Downloaded the seventh-edition djvu text from the Internet Archive item and located every hit for 0707.3793, 0904.2529 and 10.1016. Page positions were fixed by the footer digit that closes each page block in the OCR (verified against the structure "...text... / 383 / Chapter 3: ..."), not the running head. Confirmed: the footnote closing p. 384 quotes the 2009 preprint's abstract ("The new study uses 15,158 with redshifts <0.085 ... a signal exceeding 5 sigma") under the URL .../papers/0707/0707.3793.pdf, p. 9, then says "In a slightly different version of the same article" and gives 0904.2529; the footnote printed twice, closing pp. 240 and 448, reads "'Evidence for a Preferred Handedness of Spiral Galaxies,' Michael Longo, Physics Letters B 10.1016, 2009; http://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/0904/0904.2529.pdf". Finding 3's page numbers and text are exactly right. (An extra footnote closing p. 383 gives the title, "University of Michigan, 2009" and the 0707 URL — added to the docstring.)

Where I deviated. Finding 1's proposed replacement said "every re-analysis of Longo's and Shamir's own catalogues by other groups - Galaxy Zoo 2008, Hayes 2017, Iye 2021, Patel & Desmond 2024". That misdescribes two of the four: Galaxy Zoo 2008 classified its own ~37,000 SDSS spirals rather than re-analysing anyone's catalogue, and Hayes 2017 re-analysed Galaxy Zoo 1, not Longo or Shamir. Applying it verbatim would have swapped one defect for another. I used a named, closed set instead — "the four independent checks this page relies on - Galaxy Zoo 2008, Hayes 2017, Iye 2021 and Patel & Desmond 2024 ... each came back consistent with isotropy" - plus the concession sentence the finding rightly demanded.

One adjacent fix not in the findings but the same defect class: the verdict paragraph closed "the two decades of re-analysis since have gone one way", an unqualified universal of exactly the kind the TLDR finding targets, sitting one paragraph after section seven concedes the exchange is open. Narrowed to "every re-analysis listed above has gone one way - with the exchange described in section seven still open."

Both in-scope findings (1 and 2) were verified against primary sources and applied; finding 3 targets scripts/clusters.py, which I am forbidden to touch, so it is passed to the integrator in record_problems with a verified anchor.

FINDING 1 (uniqueness in tldr / section 5 / KERNEL) — CONFIRMED and applied. Kanehisa, Pawlowski & Libeskind, "Andromeda's asymmetric satellite system as a challenge to cold dark matter cosmology", is real: arXiv:2504.08047 (submitted 10 April 2025), Nature Astronomy, published 11 April 2025, DOI 10.1038/s41550-025-02480-3. Every figure the finding quotes checks out verbatim in the abstract: "All but one of Andromeda's 37 satellite galaxies are contained within 107 degrees of our Galaxy" and "less than 0.3% (0.5% when accounting for possible observational incompleteness) of Andromeda-like systems demonstrate a comparably significant asymmetry"; the 4.7-sigma figure is in the body ("The full Andromeda system is distinct from an isotropic distribution of satellites at the 4.7-sigma confidence level"), and the abstract's opening line does say "aligned towards the Milky Way". The finding's reasoning also survives checking: the paper's own robustness sections test PAndAS incompleteness (Doliva-Dolinsky detection limits) and the look-elsewhere effect explicitly, and the Milky-Way-directed rarity holds at 0.3% after look-elsewhere correction while the direction-free version rises to 4.5% (TNG) / 6.2% (EAGLE). So section 5's edge-on selection answer genuinely does not reach it, and the old "the one genuinely Earth-facing fact" was false. Applied in all three places plus a new source entry.

I did not copy the proposed answer verbatim where the source contradicted it. The paper does NOT claim the Milky Way's potential explains the lopsidedness — it says tidal effects are "unlikely to be strong enough", and that no comparable asymmetry has been reported among the Milky Way's own satellites (hedged by them as hard to ascertain given survey footprints and Galactic-disc obscuration). So the new paragraph concedes the puzzle as open and rests the answer on the referent alone, quoting their conclusion that the 6-degree alignment strongly hints at "the role of our Galaxy as significant to the formation or evolution of the lopsided Andromeda system" — the Galaxy as a mass, not as a viewpoint. In-copyright quotation from this paper across the whole entry: 38 distinct words (16 + 5 + 17), under the 60-word cap.

FINDING 2 (Tully) — CONFIRMED and applied, and it was worse than reported. I re-downloaded the same artifact (5,499,250 bytes, 134,983 lines, matching the published fingerprint) and reproduced every count. "Kroupa", "Ibata", "M31", "plane of satellites", "disk of satellites": 0 each, as published. "Tully": 2 — line 62509 "Next, galaxies in the Fisher-Tully catalogue that showed large amounts of rotation..." which is indeed inside the 72-km/s redshift-quantization passage assigned to ARG-E12, and line 100258 "caretully" (OCR for "carefully", on a page about the Pope). "Andromeda": 2, both the Italian publisher address, as published. But "dwarf" returns NINE, not the twelve the entry published — three in the redshift-quantization run (lines 62503, 62504, 62511), three in the Gulliver/Lilliputians passage (29667-29669), and three figurative (2174 "dwarfs any other", 50828 "dwarfed", 82432 "dwarfs the rest of the universe"). The finding did not catch this. Since this is the one paragraph written to be checked with a grep, I corrected both numbers, published the breakdown so each is checkable, and dated the re-verification.

FINDING 3 (clusters.py note) — the diagnosis is correct and I verified it by reading (not editing) scripts/clusters.py: line 575 still reads note="A real ΛCDM tension that has substantially deflated; with Gaia proper motions the Milky Way plane looks transient rather than rotation-supported. No geocentric content either way." That contradicts the treatment's section 1 and is now further contradicted by the 2025 Nature Astronomy paper, which postdates everything the note rests on. HARD RULE 1 forbids me editing that file, so it is in record_problems with the exact anchor and a caution that the proposed replacement text must use "ΛCDM" (the character the file actually uses) rather than the finding's "LambdaCDM".

FINDING 1 (referent) — CONFIRMED by fetching the cited URL. The University of Portsmouth / RAS release is headlined "Is Earth inside a huge void? 'Sound of the Big Bang' hints at possible solution to Hubble tension" and states in its own voice: "Earth and our solar system would need to be near the centre of a void about a billion light-years in radius and with a density about 20 per cent below the average." Our TLDR's punchline ("says 'our galaxy', not 'the Earth'") sent a reader to a page whose title appeared to refute it. Applied as the reviewer framed it: the drift is real but begins in the science communication, and the list inherited rather than invented it — which is a stronger finding for this project than the original.

FINDING 2 (15 Mpc scope) — CONFIRMED against the ar5iv full text of astro-ph/0607334, section V. Three sentences after the 15 Mpc bound: "When compared to the size of the underdensity, which according to Fig. 2 is around 1500 Mpc, this means that if we are placed at a random position inside the bubble, there is roughly a chance of 1 to 10^6..." The paper closes calling these LTB models "an exotic alternative to dark energy" (transition point d_0 = 1.34/1.68 Gpc, Table 1), so the bound is for a dark-energy-replacing bubble ~5x the ~300 Mpc void this cluster is about. per_unit.argument:
Two of three findings were mine to fix and both were real; I applied both, but finding 1's factual premise about Park et al. 2017 was itself wrong and I fixed the entry to what the paper actually says rather than to what the finding proposed. Finding 3 is a clusters.py defect I am forbidden to touch, so it goes to the integrator with a concrete, anchor-safe handoff written into my own docstring.

I downloaded and read the Park et al. 2017 PDF (AJ 153:121, MIT DSpace bitstream) rather than reasoning from memory, and it settles the disputed points. (a) The finding's claim that Park et al. "decouple the effects of beta and J2 by taking gamma from the Cassini Shapiro-delay result rather than fitting the PPN parameters and J2 together" is half right and half wrong: gamma is indeed not estimated ("Instead, we constrain the value of γ to the Cassini experiment value"; the solar angular momentum Se is likewise held to the helioseismic value), but beta and J2 ARE estimated together in one least-squares fit from the MESSENGER ranging data. (b) The actual degeneracy-breaker is stronger than either the finding or the old text: the fit does not rest on the secular residual at all. Equation 4 of the paper gives the periodic change in Mercury's argument of perihelion within a single orbit as a function of beta and gamma only, with maximum amplitude ~22.6 km against metre-level ranging, while "the periodic amplitude due to solar oblateness is several orders of magnitude smaller than the GE effect and is out of phase". So beta is read off an observable J2 barely touches. That is a direct answer to Dicke, who was arguing about the secular residual. (c) There is a genuinely Mercury-free second measurement with a number: Pijpers 1998 (MNRAS 297:L76) gets J2 = (2.18 ± 0.06) × 10⁻⁷ from the helioseismic rotation profile, and Park et al. themselves note their 2.25 × 10⁻⁷ "is in good agreement with the expected value from the helioseismology value". The old steelman's "twice, by methods that do not use Mercury" was false as written; the corrected version concedes the joint fit and then wins on the merits, which is a better page than the one that dodged.

On finding 2, I checked the arithmetic before asserting it: summing the four giant planets' maximum contributions gives 1,509,476 km = 2.17 solar radii for the largest possible solar-system barycentre excursion, and 1 AU is 99 times that. Those are the numbers now in the text.

Then added a new paragraph that concedes the joint beta/J2 fit outright and answers the circularity charge on the paper's own terms: gamma constrained to Cassini and Se to helioseismology (two of four correlated quantities imported from outside the fit), plus the periodic argument-of-perihelion swing within a single orbit, in which only beta and gamma appear, so beta is measured where J2 is not. Closes with the paper's verbatim abstract sentence (29 words, inside the 60-word in-copyright cap).

- arXiv:1009.3967v3 (published, and what the abs URL in our sources list serves): "The South Pole telescope (SPT) collaboration [18] found ΔT² < 6.5 µK²"; "the Atacama cosmology telescope (ACT) collaboration [19] found ΔT² < 8µK²"; "Hubble bubble models consistent with the SPT result have Δχ² > 209 (χ² > 814)"; "Hubble bubble models within 3σ contour have typical ΔT_H² > 10³ μK² at ℓ = 3000, two orders of magnitude larger than the SPT upper limit"; "Only those voids either with Ω₀ → 1 (Ω₀ ≳ 0.8) or z_edge → 0 (z_edge ≲ 0.2, corresponding to void radius ≲ 0.6h⁻¹Gpc) survive this test"; "The ACT result constrains |ΔH(z)/H(z)| ≲ 1% for each mass shell of radial width ∼ 1h⁻¹ Gpc".
- arXiv:1009.3967v2 (superseded): "found ΔT² < 13 µK²" for SPT, and "Hubble bubble models consistent with the ACT result have Δχ² > 195 (χ² > 800)". So the entry had imported v2 figures wholesale, and — a detail the finding did not flag — the Δχ² figure changes its ANTECEDENT between versions: v2 quotes 195 against the ACT limit, v3 quotes 209 against the SPT limit. A naive 195→209 swap while leaving the surrounding prose pointing at ACT as "the ceiling" would have introduced a new error. I rewrote the ceiling sentence so the SPT limit is the stated antecedent, which is also what the "two orders of magnitude" headline is measured against in v3.
- arXiv:1103.2335 (Ellis): confirmed verbatim, in the same paragraph as the "typical observationally viable model" specimen we already quote — "Actually you don't need a void to explain the observations; more general models can do the job [73, 31]" — and, in the same section, "Boljeko and Sussman argue [13] that the problem of improbability is ameliorated if one has for example a Szekeres rather than LTB solution." So the closing "the only version of a non-Copernican universe anybody has built" was refuted by the page's own cited source, exactly as charged.

One substantive addition beyond the findings, forced by the sources: Ellis's specimen void is quoted in the same sentence as "and no dark energy or quintessence field". So it DOES claim to displace dark energy while sitting inside the kSZ survival window. Finding 3's diagnosis is therefore right and slightly understated — the page was excluding a class in section four and illustrating the prize with a specimen that survives that particular leg of the test. I marked the specimen as caught by the supernova leg rather than the kSZ leg, which is what Zhang and Stebbins actually say about models consistent with the SPT result, and I did not write that it "does not pretend to replace dark energy", which would have been false.

Two hedge-rule guards while writing the new prose: the survival-window sentence names BOTH branches of the paper's disjunction (Ω₀ → 1 as well as z_edge → 0), not just the radius branch the proposed fix mentioned; and the section-six concession about Szekeres models is answered with a claim about what the extra freedom buys, not with a fresh unscoped universal of the kind finding 2 was raised to remove.

File is syntactically valid (ast.parse) and the ENTRY dict execs cleanly with all eleven keys intact; refutation HTML balances at 11 <p>/11 </p>, 28/28 <em>, 10/10 <strong>, 1/1 <sub>. I ran no tests, no build and no git.
